PURPOSE: The COVID-19 pandemic resulted in unprecedented disruptions to daily life, and also had significant impacts on sport participation at all levels including at the collegiate level. We aimed to describe injury incidence in National Collegiate Athletic Association men's and women's sports during the 2019/20-2020/21 seasons. METHODS: Injuries reported to the NCAA Injury Surveillance Program (ISP) by athletic trainers during 2019/20 -2020/21 were analyzed. Injury incidence (rates per 1,000 athlete exposures (AEs)) was examined overall and by sport, event type (practices/competitions) and division. B ayesian Negative Binomial models were used to estimate injury rates, with estimated incidence and differential incidence presented in terms of posterior means and 95% Cred ible Intervals (Cred. Int.). Prevalences of the most reported specific injuries were expressed as frequencies (%s). RESULTS: During 2019/20-2020/21, the NCAA ISP recorded 15,780 injuries and 2,053,724 AEs in men’s sports, and 7,685 injuries and 1,197,045 AEs in wom en’s sports. We determined the posterior mean overall rate to be 8.28 per 1, 000 AEs (95% Cred. Int.: 5.59, 13.18) in men’s sports and 6.99 per 1,000 AEs (95% Cred. Int.: 4.64, 11.38) in women’s sports. Estimated injury incidence was higher in competitions than practices in men’s (Posterior mean Ratio: 3.49; 95% Cred. Int.: 1.84, 6.09) and women’s (Posterior mean Ratio: 2.11; 95% Cred. Int.: 1.11, 3.68) sports. Among all men’s sports, overall injury incidence was highest in men’s football (Posterior mean= 12.14 per 1,000 AEs; 95% Cred. Int.: 8.09, 19.75), and among all women’s sport s, it was highest in women’s gymnastics (Posterior mean= 18.61 per 1,000 AEs; 95% Cred. Int.: 12.13, 29.93). Lateral ankle sprains and concussions were the most commonly reported injuries in b oth groups

While the types of injuries and affected body parts show some similariti es, there was a lower incidence rate at the Accra Games. These findings provide valuable epidemiological data to inform injury prevention strategies for para sports in A frica, especially in low to middle- income countries. (No relevant relationships reported) In the NCAA, fall and spring sports are defined by the semester of the ir championship season, but they also have a non-championship season during the opposite semester. Transitioning into the championship and non-championship seasons involves an acute increase in physical activity associated with a greater injury rate. No study has examined the injury risk associated with the timing of transition periods related to fall versus spring sport annual cycles. PURPOSE: To quantify and compare injury incidence rates (IR) between NCAA Division I fall and spring sports during the tran sition into championship and non- championship seasons. METHODS: Injury data collected from ten Olympic sports (excluding American Football) were analyzed retrospectively alongside participa tion and seasonal transition dates from institutional records. Injuries in the first two weeks of each season were described using frequency, proportion, and IR based on 1000 athlete - days. Relative and IR risks with 95% confidence intervals were calculated to compare seasonal transition periods. We aimed to describe injury incidence in National Collegiate Athletic Association men's and women's sports during the 2019/20-2020/21 seasons. METHODS: Injuries reported to the NCAA Injury Surveillance Program (ISP) by athletic trainers during 2019/20 -2020/21 were analyzed. Injury incidence (rates per 1,000 athlete exposures (AEs)) was examined overall and by sport, event type (practices/competitions) and division. B ayesian Negative Binomial models were used to estimate injury rates, with estimated incidence and differential incidence presented in terms of posterior means and 95% Cred ible Intervals (Cred. Int.). Prevalences of the most reported specific injuries were expressed as frequencies (%s). RESULTS: During 2019/20-2020/21, the NCAA ISP recorded 15,780 injuries and 2,053,724 AEs in men’s sports, and 7,685 injuries and 1,197,045 AEs in wom en’s sports. We determined the posterior mean overall rate to be 8.28 per 1, 000 AEs (95% Cred. Int.: 5.59, 13.18) in men’s sports and 6.99 per 1,000 AEs (95% Cred. Int.: 4.64, 11.38) in women’s sports. Estimated injury incidence was higher in competitions than practices in men’s (Posterior mean Ratio: 3.49; 95% Cred. Int.: 1.84, 6.09) and women’s (Posterior mean Ratio: 2.11; 95% Cred. Int.: 1.11, 3.68) sports. Among all men’s sports, overall injury incidence was highest in men’s football (Posterior mean= 12.14 per 1,000 AEs; 95% Cred. Int.: 8.09, 19.75), and among all women’s sport s, it was highest in women’s gymnastics (Posterior mean= 18.61 per 1,000 AEs; 95% Cred. Int.: 12.13, 29.93). Lateral ankle sprains and concussions were the most commonly reported injuries in b oth groups. CONCLUSIONS: Injury incidence during the study period remained consistent with historical patterns, with higher rates observed in contact/collision sports and during competitions relative to practices. Common injuries also aligned with previous observations in this population. As pan demic-related disruptions impacted sports differently during this period, future efforts may examine injury incidence in juxtaposition to specific scheduling di sruptions to identify potential patterns.
